query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Because local atomic environments (i.e. lattice distortions from mass, size, and electronegativity mismatches) largely determine phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys, a predictive approach that explicitly quantifies such local chemical fluctuations will more accurately identify alloys with low lattice (phonon) thermal conductivity than methods that rely solely on average or bulk parameters.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equimolar high-entropy alloy (e.g. a five‐element system such as FeCoCrMnNi or similar composition) that exhibits moderate lattice distortions and has been considered for thermal-insulation applications under ambient conditions.
generation.intervention: Implement the predictive approach by calculating, from first principles or via machine-learned force fields, the local chemical and strain field fluctuations caused by differences in atomic mass, size, and electronegativity. Use these detailed metrics as descriptors in the model to predict enhanced phonon scattering and thereby lower thermal conductivity.
generation.conditions: The predictive model operates under ambient to moderately high temperature conditions relevant to thermal-insulation applications. The model’s predictions are compared to standard empirical methods; subsequent experimental validation is done using techniques (e.g., time-domain thermoreflectance at room and elevated temperatures) to measure lattice thermal conductivity.
generation.structural_mediator: The enhanced local lattice distortions (i.e. increased magnitude of force-constant fluctuations) which shorten phonon mean free paths due to intensified phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: By capturing the effects of local disorder — specifically, elemental mismatches that yield severe lattice distortions — the approach predicts lower phonon velocities and shorter phonon lifetimes. This in turn decreases the intrinsic thermal conductivity, making it a superior predictor over models that average out such local effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to predictions from conventional models, the new approach will forecast a significantly lower phonon thermal conductivity in alloys with pronounced local lattice distortions. Experimentally, alloys identified by the approach as ‘low-κL’ should show lower measured phonon thermal conductivity relative to the baseline predicted values.
generation.baseline: Current prediction methods that average bulk properties (e.g., Debye temperature correlations or simple mixing rules) without explicitly accounting for the detailed local distortions.
generation.boundary: The approach should be applicable only to high-entropy alloys with a substantial number (four or more) of principal elements having significant differences in atomic mass, size, or electronegativity. Its predictive advantage may diminish for alloys with nearly homogeneous constituent properties or where additional microstructural factors (e.g., extreme porosity, secondary phase precipitations) dominate the thermal transport.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitatively, the magnitude of the improvement is uncertain; the hypothesis anticipates a notable, though not precisely defined, better agreement with experimental values. Variations in processing or extrinsic defects could also affect the measurements, adding uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of high-entropy alloys that systematically vary in elemental mismatches (thus altering the degree of predicted local lattice distortion). Use the new predictive approach to forecast their phonon thermal conductivities. Then, measure the lattice thermal conductivity (isolating the phonon contribution) over the relevant temperature range using techniques such as time-domain thermoreflectance or laser flash analysis. Compare the experimental results with both the new model and conventional predictions.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of local lattice distortions (e.g. via high-resolution diffraction or spectroscopic techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured phonon thermal conductivities do not show a closer correlation to the predictions made by the new approach than to those made by traditional averaged models—or if alloys predicted to have low phonon conductivity do not exhibit statistically significant lower values—the hypothesis is falsified.

In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. cited_evidence.text: Using the same approach, the value of κL was computed for various temperatures in the range 300–700 K (Figure 9). At 300 K, the κL value is 0.4 W K−1 m−1, which is a very low value of the lattice thermal conductivity, favorable for thermoelectric materials. This is due to the lattice distortion effect of high-entropy alloys that can reduce phonon velocity and enhance phonon scattering, resulting in low thermal conductivity. Additionally, one can observe that when the temperature rises, the thermal conductivity of the lattice decreases, which is also due to an increase in phonon scattering at higher temperatures.
